By Malcolm Davidson

The dollar climbed to 2-1/2 year highs against the yen on Monday, boosted by renewed signs of a faltering Japanese economic recovery and a widening gap between interest rates in the United States and Japan.
The dollar peaked at 111.66 yen in European trading hours after investors began to liquidate long yen positions and analysts saw signs of growing investment abroad by Japanese institutions.

The weekend meeting of Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations in Washington also underpinned the U.S. currency with finance ministers and central bank chiefs expressing satisfaction with current exchange rates.

"There seems to be a view in Japan they're not going to have huge capital losses by being in overseas assets -- they don't see the yen gaining by too much and they're just going for high yields," said Pat Magill, head of Daiwa Europe's corporate desk.
By the close of business in Europe, the dollar was quoted at at 111.63 yen and 1.5270 marks, compared with Friday's late European levels of 110.78 yen and 1.5239 marks.
European share markets began the week in a subdued mood, but London and Paris both reversed early weakness and French shares ended the day more than one percent higher.
Paris was helped higher by a firm Wall Street, with the Dow Jones Average up nearly 25 points as European bourses closed. Frankfurt remained weak, however.
Gold came back under pressure on both sides of the Atlantic after being fixed at its lowest level in a year.
After falling through the key $380 level in the morning, gold closed at $378.60, compared with Friday's $380.15.
Bearish sentiment seen on Friday deepened during the day, but traders said the slide could spark a market bounce.
Japan's economic prospects provided the major impetus for the dollar after August preliminary industrial output figures showed a larger-than-expected decline of 1.9 percent.
Weekend comments by Japan's Finance Minister Wataru Kubo and Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita were seen encouraging Japanese institutional investors to seek higher returns overseas.
"There is a lot of talk of a substantial amount of capital flowing out of Japan in the second half of the fiscal year which starts Tuesday," said a currency dealer at a German bank in London.
The London stock market ended the third trading quarter modestly higher on the day after reversing early losses. The FTSE 100 share index closed 7.3 points up at 3,953.7.
The FTSE's gain over the quarter was 242.7 points, almost the entire year's rise for the blue-chip indicator.

"It's been a good quarter for London...sterling performed well and company results have been healthy...now people are peering over into the fourth quarter to see what they are going to do," one trader said.
French traders cited Wall Street and September futures expiring in a bullish mood for the 25.76 point rise in the CAC 40 index.

Eurotunnel shares were suspended in Paris, London and Brussels at the company's request as talks between the Channel Tunnel operator and its creditor banks went down to the wire. Eurotunnel is seeking to refinance $14 billion of debt.
German shares ended bourse trade lower amid evidence of profit-taking. The 30-share blue chip DAX index ended down 7.19 points, or 0.27 percent, at 2,651.85 points.

Dealers blamed the fall on a mild bout of profit-taking after the DAX surged to record highs last week, but said many investors steered clear of the market in the absence of any significant corporate news.
CURRENCIES AT 1600 GMT
The dollar was trading at 111.63 yen and 1.5270 marks, compared with Friday's late European levels of 110.78 yen and 1.5239 marks.
